subject: Banking
title: The Keating Five Scandal
description: A quick, practical guide to The Keating Five Scandal.

hook.text: Five US senators accepted $1.3 million from banker Charles Keating.

buildup.text: Keating ran Lincoln Savings and Loan. He used depositors' money on junk bonds and luxury real estate projects.

discovery.text: When regulators investigated, Keating called his senators. They held a meeting pressuring the regulators to back off.

twist.text: Lincoln Savings collapsed in 1989. 23,000 depositors lost savings. Keating went to prison.

climax.text: The Keating Five showed how money buys political protection for bad banking.

punchline.text: $1.3 million in donations. Five senators pressured regulators.

quiz.question: What did the five senators do for Charles Keating?
options: Pressured regulators to stop investigating his S&L

details.summary: Five US senators intervened with regulators on behalf of savings and loan owner Charles Keating, who had donated $1.3 million to their campaigns. Keating's Lincoln Savings ultimately cost taxpayers $3.4 billion when it failed.
details.whyItMatters: The Keating Five scandal exposed how campaign donations could buy political protection for reckless banking. It demonstrated the dangerous intersection of money in politics and financial regulation.
takeaways: Five senators pressured regulators to delay enforcement against Lincoln Savings
Keating donated $1.3 million to their campaigns through various channels
Lincoln Savings' failure cost taxpayers $3.4 billion

faq.question: What did the Keating Five senators actually do?
faq.answer: The five senators attended meetings with bank regulators and pressured them to back off their investigation of Lincoln Savings. The regulatory delays allowed Keating to continue risky activities, ultimately increasing the cost of the failure significantly.

faq.question: Were the senators punished?
faq.answer: The Senate Ethics Committee reprimanded one senator, Alan Cranston, and found the others had shown poor judgment but committed no crime. John McCain, one of the five, became a prominent campaign finance reform advocate partly in response to the scandal.
